days.title: Reactions That Produce & Consume ATP
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Identify reactions that produce ATP.
  • Identify reactions that consume ATP.
  • Explain the ATP-ADP cycle.
  • Relate ATP turnover to cell activity.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • ATP-ADP cycle — continuous regeneration of ATP.
  • Substrate-level phosphorylation — direct ATP formation.
  • Oxidative phosphorylation — ATP via ETC + chemiosmosis.
  • Photophosphorylation — ATP via light-driven ETC.

📚 Lesson Content

A. ATP-Producing Reactions

  • Glycolysis (substrate-level)
  • Krebs cycle (substrate-level)
  • Oxidative phosphorylation (ETC + chemiosmosis) — the biggest producer
  • Light reactions (photophosphorylation)

B. ATP-Consuming Reactions

  • Calvin cycle (uses ATP + NADPH)
  • Active transport (Na⁺/K⁺ pump)
  • Muscle contraction
  • Protein synthesis
  • Cell division

C. ATP Turnover

A typical cell uses and regenerates ~10 million ATP molecules per second. ATP is not stored — it is generated on demand.

💬 Let's Discuss

Think of ATP as cash in a cell's wallet. Some processes earn ATP (they make it from ADP + Pi), and many more spend it. Sorting them correctly is the key skill this week.

ATP-producing processes: Glycolysis makes a net 2 ATP per glucose by substrate-level phosphorylation. The Krebs cycle makes 2 more ATP per glucose the same way. Oxidative phosphorylation (ETC + chemiosmosis in mitochondria) makes by far the most, because it cashes in all the NADH and FADH₂. In plants, photophosphorylation in the thylakoids makes ATP using light energy.

ATP-consuming processes: the Calvin cycle spends ATP (and NADPH) to build sugar. Active transport, such as the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, spends ATP to move ions uphill. Muscle contraction spends ATP each time myosin pulls on actin; after death, ATP runs out and muscles lock in place (rigor mortis). Protein synthesis spends energy to link each amino acid. Even the first steps of glycolysis spend 2 ATP before earning 4.

A good rule: breaking down fuel molecules (catabolism) usually releases energy and makes ATP; building molecules, moving things and doing mechanical work (anabolism and work) usually consumes it. Note that photosynthesis as a whole stores energy: the light reactions make ATP, but the Calvin cycle immediately spends it, so the plant gains sugar, not spare ATP.

Common mistake: saying the ETC "uses" ATP. The ETC uses the energy of electrons to build an H⁺ gradient, which ATP synthase then uses to make ATP.

pairs.why: Glycolysis makes a net 2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.
The Krebs cycle makes 2 ATP per glucose (1 per turn).
Oxidative phosphorylation makes most of the ATP using the ETC.
Photophosphorylation makes ATP using light energy in thylakoids.
The Calvin cycle spends ATP to build sugar.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump spends ATP to move ions against their gradients.

takeaways: ATP is produced in glycolysis, Krebs cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and photophosphorylation.
ATP is consumed in the Calvin cycle, active transport, muscle contraction, and biosynthesis.
ATP turnover is rapid — ATP is generated on demand.
The ATP-ADP cycle maintains cellular energy balance.

days.title: ATP Accounting in Respiration
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Compute ATP yield per stage of respiration.
  • Explain why the total is ~36–38 ATP, not 40.
  • Account for ATP used in transport.
  • Interpret ATP yield tables.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • ATP yield — total ATP produced per glucose.
  • NADH — carries 2.5 ATP each (in ETC).
  • FADH₂ — carries 1.5 ATP each.
  • Shuttle cost — 2 ATP used to move NADH into mitochondria.

📚 Lesson Content

ATP Yield Table (per glucose)

StageATPNADHFADH₂
Glycolysis220
Pyruvate oxidation020
Krebs cycle262
Subtotal4102

ETC ATP Conversion

  • 10 NADH × 2.5 ATP = 25 ATP
  • 2 FADH₂ × 1.5 ATP = 3 ATP
  • Substrate-level = 4 ATP
  • Total = 32 ATP (modern estimate)
  • Older textbooks say 36–38 (using 3 ATP/NADH)

💬 Let's Discuss

How many ATP does one glucose really give? Let us count, step by step, like doing a budget.

Direct ATP (substrate-level): glycolysis, net 2; Krebs cycle, 2 (one per turn). Total = 4 ATP.

Electron carriers: glycolysis gives 2 NADH; pyruvate oxidation gives 2 NADH; the Krebs cycle gives 6 NADH and 2 FADH₂. Total = 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂.

Cashing in at the ETC: modern measurements show each NADH yields about 2.5 ATP and each FADH₂ about 1.5 ATP (FADH₂ enters the chain at a later point, so it pumps fewer H⁺). So 10 × 2.5 = 25, plus 2 × 1.5 = 3, giving 28 ATP from oxidative phosphorylation.

Grand total: 4 + 28 = about 32 ATP per glucose.

Why do older books say 36–38? They used whole-number values (3 ATP per NADH, 2 per FADH₂), which give 38. Later research found the ratios are not whole numbers, that some H⁺ leaks across the membrane, and that energy is spent moving ATP and pyruvate across mitochondrial membranes — so the real yield is closer to 30–32. You may see either answer; what matters is understanding the method.

Compare with fermentation: only 2 ATP per glucose. Aerobic respiration is about 16 times more efficient, capturing roughly a third of glucose's energy as ATP; the rest is released as heat, which helps keep our bodies warm.

Common mistake: forgetting the 2 NADH from pyruvate oxidation, which makes the total come out too low.

pairs.why: Glycolysis gives 2 net ATP and 2 NADH.
Pyruvate oxidation makes no ATP but gives 2 NADH per glucose.
Two Krebs turns give 2 ATP, 6 NADH and 2 FADH₂.
Each NADH yields about 2.5 ATP in the ETC.
Each FADH₂ yields about 1.5 ATP because it enters later in the chain.
4 direct ATP + 28 from the ETC ≈ 32 ATP.

days.title: ATP Accounting in Photosynthesis
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Compute ATP and NADPH used in the Calvin cycle.
  • Explain the ATP/NADPH ratio needed.
  • Compare ATP usage in photosynthesis vs respiration.
  • Summarize photosynthesis energetics.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Calvin cycle cost — 18 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose.
  • Ratio — 3 ATP : 2 NADPH per CO₂ fixed.
  • Photophosphorylation — ATP production in light reactions.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Calvin Cycle Cost (per glucose)

  • 6 CO₂ fixed
  • 18 ATP used
  • 12 NADPH used
  • Produces 1 glucose

B. Per CO₂ Fixed

  • 3 ATP
  • 2 NADPH

C. ATP/NADPH Ratio

The light reactions must produce ATP and NADPH in a 3:2 ratio to match the Calvin cycle's needs.

💬 Let's Discuss

Photosynthesis also has a budget, but it runs in the opposite direction: instead of earning ATP from glucose, the plant spends ATP and NADPH to build glucose.

Each time the Calvin cycle fixes one CO₂, it uses 3 ATP and 2 NADHP. Glucose has six carbons, so to make one glucose the plant must fix 6 CO₂. Multiply by six: 6 × 3 = 18 ATP and 6 × 2 = 12 NADPH. That is an ATP:NADPH ratio of 3:2.

Where does the ATP go? Some is spent in the reduction phase (converting fixed carbon into G3P, along with all the NADPH), and the rest in the regeneration phase (rebuilding RuBP so the cycle can continue). Every turn of the cycle must rebuild its starting molecule, so a share of the energy goes to "maintenance," not to new sugar.

The light reactions must supply this mix. Linear electron flow makes ATP and NADPH in roughly equal amounts, which is a little short on ATP. Plants solve this with cyclic electron flow around Photosystem I, which makes extra ATP without making NADPH.

Compare the two budgets: building one glucose costs 18 ATP + 12 NADPH, while breaking it down aerobically returns only about 32 ATP. Energy is lost as heat at each conversion — a reminder that no energy transfer in living things is 100% efficient.

Problem-solving tip: always convert to "per CO₂" first (3 ATP, 2 NADPH), then multiply. For example, 12 CO₂ need 36 ATP and 24 NADPH, and give 2 glucose.

pairs.why: Making one glucose uses 6 × 3 = 18 ATP.
Making one glucose uses 6 × 2 = 12 NADPH.
Six CO₂ provide the six carbons of one glucose.
18 ATP : 12 NADPH simplifies to 3:2.
Six turns of the cycle produce enough G3P for one glucose.

days.title: Oxygen's Role & Anaerobic Pathways
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Explain the role of oxygen in respiration.
  • Describe electron flow without oxygen.
  • Explain fermentation pathways.
  • Compare anaerobic vs aerobic energetics.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • O₂ — final electron acceptor in ETC.
  • Anaerobic respiration — ETC without O₂ (using other acceptors).
  • Fermentation — regenerates NAD⁺ without ETC.
  • Lactate / ethanol — fermentation end products.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Oxygen's Role

  • Accepts electrons at the end of ETC
  • Combines with H⁺ → H₂O
  • Keeps ETC running
  • Without O₂: ETC halts → NADH accumulates

B. Anaerobic Pathways

PathwayEnd ProductWhere
Lactic acid fermentationLactateMuscle cells, bacteria (yogurt)
Alcoholic fermentationEthanol + CO₂Yeast, some bacteria

C. Why Fermentation Matters

Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue producing 2 ATP per glucose — enough for short bursts of activity.

💬 Let's Discuss

Why do we die within minutes without oxygen? Because oxygen does a single, irreplaceable job: it is the final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain. It pulls electrons off the last protein complex and combines with H⁺ to form water. Without it, the chain backs up like a blocked drain: electrons have nowhere to go, the H⁺ pumps stop, ATP synthase stops, NADH cannot be turned back into NAD⁺, and the Krebs cycle halts.

Only glycolysis can continue — but it needs NAD⁺ too. That is where fermentation comes in. Its purpose is not to make extra ATP; it is to regenerate NAD⁺ by passing NADH's electrons to pyruvate (or a product of it). In lactic acid fermentation, pyruvate becomes lactate (in muscles during intense exercise and in lactobacilli). In alcoholic fermentation, pyruvate becomes ethanol and CO₂ (in yeast). Either way, the cell gets only the 2 ATP from glycolysis.

Some bacteria and archaea do something different called anaerobic respiration: they still run an ETC, but use another final electron acceptor such as nitrate or sulfate instead of oxygen. Bacteria in mangrove mud and deep soil do this, producing the rotten-egg smell of hydrogen sulfide. Don't confuse this with fermentation, which uses no ETC at all.

After a sprint, you keep breathing hard: this "oxygen debt" provides oxygen to convert lactate back to pyruvate and restore ATP. Common mistake: thinking oxygen becomes the CO₂ we exhale. The CO₂ comes from the carbons of glucose; oxygen ends up in water.

pairs.why: Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the ETC.
Oxygen + electrons + H⁺ form water.
Anaerobic respiration uses an ETC with a different final acceptor, like nitrate or sulfate.
Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.
Lactate is the product of lactic acid fermentation.
Alcoholic fermentation makes ethanol and CO₂.
